summary: A Hebrew question with a question word is the statement with the question word put first: הַנֶּהָג פֹּה “the driver is here” → אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג? “where is the driver?”. There is no auxiliary verb and, in the present, no “is / are” at all: מָה אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? “what (do) you want?”, מִי הִיא? “who (is) she?”. The question words: מָה what, מִי who, אֵיפֹה where (לְאָן where to, מֵאֵיפֹה where from), מָתַי when, אֵיךְ how, לָמָּה why (everyday) and מַדּוּעַ why (formal), כַּמָּה how many / how much (with a plural noun), אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ / אֵילוּ which (agreeing with the noun, which follows it), and the two-word שֶׁל מִי whose. A preposition always goes in front of the question word, never to the end of the sentence: עִם מִי? “who with?”, מֵאֵיפֹה? “where from?”, לְמִי? “to whom?”. In speech the question word may also stay at the end as an echo (הַתִּיק שֶׁל מִי?), but the normal place is first.

head: question word
meaning
example
rows: מָה אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? — What do you (m.) want?
מִי הָרוֹפֵא? — Who is the doctor?
אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג? — Where is the driver?
מָתַי אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב? — When is dinner?
אֵיךְ הַמָּרָק? — How is the soup?
לָמָּה אַתָּה לֹא אוֹכֵל? — Why aren’t you eating?
how many, how much (+ plural noun)
כַּמָּה יְלָדִים יֵשׁ לָהּ? — How many children does she have?
אֵיזוֹ כּוֹס שֶׁלְּךָ? — Which glass is yours?
שֶׁל מִי הַתִּיק הַזֶּה? — Whose bag is this?
blocks.caption: The question words of lesson 10 — each goes first in its question.

head: with a preposition
meaning
blocks.caption: The preposition comes first — it is never left at the end of the question.

blocks.title: Question word first — then the statement
blocks.text: Take the statement, put the question word in front, and change nothing else: הִיא רוֹצָה קָפֶה → מָה הִיא רוֹצָה? No “do”, no inversion, and no “is” in the present.

blocks.title: “Which” agrees with the noun
blocks.text: אֵיזֶה סֵפֶר (m.), אֵיזוֹ כּוֹס (f.), אֵילוּ סְפָרִים (plural). In everyday speech you will hear אֵיזֶה for everything — but write אֵיזוֹ before a feminine noun.

blocks.title: כַּמָּה takes a plural
blocks.text: כַּמָּה יְלָדִים? — never *כַּמָּה יֶלֶד. (Arabic كَمْ takes a singular — the opposite.) Without a question mark, כַּמָּה סְפָרִים means “a few books”.

blocks.title: Two words for “why”
blocks.text: לָמָּה is what everyone says; מַדּוּעַ is formal — the news, a teacher, an official letter. Both mean exactly “why”.

blocks.title: Where, where to, where from
blocks.text: אֵיפֹה asks where something is. With movement: לְאָן? “where to?” and מֵאֵיפֹה? “where from?” — just like German Wo? Wohin? Woher? (lessons 11 and 13).

items.title: Chinese
points: the question word stays where the answer would be

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you ask
questions: What do I want to know: a thing, a person, a place, a time, a manner, a reason, a number, a choice, an owner?
Is there a preposition? Put it before the question word.
“Which” — is the noun masculine, feminine or plural?
Is it everyday speech (לָמָּה) or formal (מַדּוּעַ)?

askYourself: What am I asking about? a thing → מָה; a person → מִי; a place → אֵיפֹה (where to → לְאָן, where from → מֵאֵיפֹה); a time → מָתַי; a manner → אֵיךְ; a reason → לָמָּה (formal מַדּוּעַ); a number or amount → כַּמָּה; a choice → אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ / אֵילוּ; an owner → שֶׁל מִי.
Does a preposition belong to the question word (with, to, from, for, about)? → put it in front: עִם מִי, לְמִי, מֵאֵיפֹה.
Is it “which + noun”? → אֵיזֶה before a masculine noun, אֵיזוֹ before a feminine one, אֵילוּ before a plural.
Is it “how many”? → כַּמָּה + plural noun.
Did I add “is / are” or “do”? → take it out: Hebrew has neither in a present question.
Is the rest in statement order? → it should be: מָה אַתָּה רוֹצֶה?
steps: Choose the question word (with its preposition).
Put it first; keep the rest; end with “?”.

traps: No “do” and no “is”: “Where is the driver?” = אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?
אֵיפֹה is “where (at)”; “where to” is לְאָן and “where from” is מֵאֵיפֹה.
אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ / אֵילוּ agree with the noun after them.
“What is your name?” is asked with “how”: אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ?
A preposition cannot be left at the end: “Who are you with?” = עִם מִי אַתָּה?
מַדּוּעַ is correct but formal; in conversation say לָמָּה.

quiz.why: The question word goes first and there is no verb “is” in the present.

quiz.q: Which word asks about a reason in a formal letter?
quiz.why: מַדּוּעַ is the formal “why”; לָמָּה is the everyday one. מָתַי is “when”, אֵיךְ “how”.

quiz.q: Complete: ___ כּוֹס שֶׁלְּךָ? (“Which glass is yours?”)
quiz.why: כּוֹס is feminine, so “which” is אֵיזוֹ; אֵיזֶה is masculine and אֵילוּ plural.

quiz.q: “Who are you going with?” — where does עִם go?
quiz.why: A Hebrew preposition always stands before its word — also before a question word.

quiz.q: כַּמָּה ___ יֵשׁ לָהּ? (“How many children does she have?”)
quiz.why: After כַּמָּה the noun is plural and has no article.

quiz.q: How do you ask “What is your name?” (to a man)?
quiz.why: Literally “how do they call you?” — with אֵיךְ, as in Greek Πώς σε λένε; and German Wie heißt du?

seeAlso.note: Arabic also puts the question word first, and several are the same words: מָתַי = مَتَى, כַּמָּה ≈ كَمْ, מָה = مَا. But Arabic كَمْ takes a singular noun (كَمْ وَلَدًا) where Hebrew takes a plural.
German W-questions also start with the question word, but the verb must come second (Wo ist …?); Hebrew has no verb at all in a present question.
Chinese leaves the question word where the answer goes (你去哪儿？); Hebrew moves it to the front.

notes.text: As in Russian, the question word comes first and there is no “is” in the present (Где водитель? ~ אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?). Куда / откуда match לְאָן / מֵאֵיפֹה.
Greek also puts the question word first (Πού είναι ο οδηγός;); Hebrew has no verb “is” in the present: אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?
As in Spanish, the question word goes first and a preposition goes before it (¿con quién? ~ עִם מִי?); unlike Spanish, there is no verb “is” in the present: אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?
English uses “do” and can leave a preposition at the end (“Who is it for?”); Hebrew has no “do”, no “is” in the present, and the preposition always goes first: בִּשְׁבִיל מִי?
As in French, the question word comes first and a preposition stays with it (avec qui ? ~ עִם מִי?); Hebrew needs no est-ce que and no inversion.
German also puts the question word first and has wo / wohin / woher ~ אֵיפֹה / לְאָן / מֵאֵיפֹה; but Hebrew does not put the verb second — the statement order stays.
Hindi keeps the question word in place (ड्राइवर कहाँ है?); Hebrew puts it first: אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?
Persian usually keeps the question word where the answer would be (راننده کجاست؟); Hebrew moves it to the front.
Marathi keeps the question word where the answer goes (ड्रायव्हर कुठे आहे?); Hebrew puts it first and adds no verb.

Arabic also puts the question word first (أَيْنَ السَّائِقُ؟) and needs no verb in the present; several words are cognates: מִי ~ مَنْ, מָה ~ مَا, כַּמָּה ~ كَمْ — but كَمْ takes a singular noun and כַּמָּה a plural.
Turkish keeps the question word in place (Şoför nerede?); Hebrew moves it to the front: אֵיפֹה הַנֶּהָג?
Japanese keeps the question word in place and adds か (運転手はどこですか); Hebrew puts it first and adds nothing.
Korean keeps the question word in place (운전기사는 어디에 있어요?); Hebrew puts it first.
Finnish also puts the question word first (Missä kuljettaja on?) and has three “where” words like Hebrew: missä / mihin / mistä ~ אֵיפֹה / לְאָן / מֵאֵיפֹה.
Hungarian puts the question word first, right before the verb (Hol van a sofőr?), and has hol / hova / honnan ~ אֵיפֹה / לְאָן / מֵאֵיפֹה.
Swahili keeps the question word in place, often after the verb (dereva yuko wapi?); Hebrew puts it first.
Luganda usually keeps the question word after the verb (ogenda wa? “where are you going?”); Hebrew puts it first: לְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ?
Chinese keeps the question word where the answer goes (司机在哪儿？); Hebrew moves it to the front and needs no 在.
Vietnamese keeps the question word in place (tài xế ở đâu?); Hebrew moves it to the front.
Inuktitut question words (kina “who”, suna “what”) take case endings, and the verb takes an interrogative ending; Hebrew puts the question word first and leaves the verb unchanged.
